title: App Store review times in 2026: Apple vs Google Play
summary: App Store review times in 2026: how long review takes, the best day to submit and what to do if you get stuck.
body_markdown:
## App Store review time in 2026


You've fixed the bug, signed the build and hit Submit for Review. Now you wait. Apple says it reviews at least half of submissions within 24 hours and[90% within 48 hours](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/) . Google Play usually finishes in[under an hour](https://www.runway.team/playstorereviewtimes) .


But your users only see the update once it goes live, and that can be well after review ends. Across iOS updates shipped by teams using Bitrise this year, the typical release went live about a day after submission, and roughly one in three took more than three days.


Below, we look at why Apple's queue slowed down in 2026, which days to submit on, what to do when a build is stuck in review, and how React Native teams ship urgent fixes without waiting for review at all.


**Apple App Store** **Google Play**


**What the stores say** At least half reviewed within 24 hours,[90% within 48 hours](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/) .[1.5 days on average](https://mobilegamer.biz/app-store-review-times-are-being-dragged-down-by-a-flood-of-ai-made-apps-and-games/) , 14 hours for minor updates[Up to seven days for some apps](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9859751?hl=en)


**Queue plus review (Runway)**[About 15 hours waiting](https://www.runway.team/appreviewtimes) , plus 49 minutes in review[About 47 minutes](https://www.runway.team/playstorereviewtimes)


**Submission to live (Bitrise)** About 25 hours. 49% live within a day, 61% within two Not measured


Apple's and Runway's figures stop the clock when review finishes. Ours keeps running until the update is live in the store, so it also counts any time a team holds an approved build before releasing it. Your release date depends on that number.


Most of the wait happens before anyone looks at your app.["Waiting for Review"](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-information/app-and-submission-statuses) in App Store Connect means Apple has accepted your submission, but nobody has picked it up yet. Once a build moves to "In Review", it's usually done in[under an hour](https://www.runway.team/appreviewtimes) .


TestFlight has its own queue. Builds for external testers go through Beta App Review first, while internal testers skip it, and later builds of the same version may not need a full review. In late October, Runway's tracker showed[about 11 hours waiting](https://www.runway.team/appreviewtimes) and an hour in review, so give yourself around half a day before testers can install a new build.


## Why Apple's review queue is slower in 2026


Apple's review queue is busier than it's ever been. New app submissions jumped this year, Apple moved its 90% target from 24 hours to 48, and it now reviews updates to existing apps ahead of new ones, which helps if you're shipping an update.


### New app submissions surged


The Information reported[235,800 new apps](https://gizmodo.com/apple-app-store-experiences-surge-in-new-apps-amid-vibe-coding-boom-2000742653) on the App Store in Q1 2026, up 84% on a year earlier. That came after[about 600,000 new apps](https://www.mactech.com/2026/07/20/the-number-of-new-apps-released-in-the-app-store-grew-30-to-about-600000-last-year/) in 2025, itself a 30% rise. Mobilegamer.biz links the jump to[AI-made apps and games](https://mobilegamer.biz/app-store-review-times-are-being-dragged-down-by-a-flood-of-ai-made-apps-and-games/) , and Apple told the site it handled an average of 378,000 submissions a week over the 12 weeks to mid-October.


### Apple's 24-hour promise became 48 hours


For years, Apple said it reviewed 90% of submissions within a day. Its[App Review page](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/) now says 90% within two days, with at least half inside one.


### Updates to existing apps go first


Apple told Mobilegamer.biz[it prioritizes updates](https://mobilegamer.biz/app-store-review-times-are-being-dragged-down-by-a-flood-of-ai-made-apps-and-games/) to existing apps, and that some new apps need extra checks and take longer. Developers quoted by Michael Tsai describe[waits of three to seven days](https://mjtsai.com/blog/2026/03/02/mac-app-store-review-times-increasing/) , with Mac apps hit hardest. People tend to post when things go wrong, so treat these as the worst cases.


## How long iOS updates take to go live


The typical iOS update went live about 25 hours after it was submitted for review. About half were live within a day, but one in three took longer than three days. These figures cover releases shipped by teams using[Bitrise Release Management](https://bitrise.io/platform/release-management) between January and September 2026.


**Releases** **Time from submission to live**


Fastest 25% Under 12 hours


Typical (median) About 25 hours


Slowest 25% More than four days


Overall, 49% of releases were live within a day, 61% within two days and 69% within three. The most recent three months looked the same, so things haven't improved.


### Why our number is higher than Apple's


Apple says minor updates take[14 hours on average](https://mobilegamer.biz/app-store-review-times-are-being-dragged-down-by-a-flood-of-ai-made-apps-and-games/) to review, and Runway's tracker showed[about 16 hours](https://www.runway.team/appreviewtimes) of queue plus review in late October. Most of the extra time in our data is the gap between approval and release, because teams choose when to ship an approved build.


### Rejections rarely cause the delay


Fewer than 2% of releases were resubmitted, so for most teams the queue is the thing to plan around. When a resubmission does happen, it costs more than the time it takes to fix the issue, because the build goes back through review from the start.


All of these are updates to apps already on the store. We don't have data on brand-new apps, which Apple says can take longer.


## What's the best day to submit an iOS update?


Monday to Thursday. Updates submitted on those days went live in about a day. Friday submissions took nearly four, mostly because they sat until Monday or Tuesday. Submitting between 06:00 and 18:00 UTC helped too.


**Day submitted (UTC)** **Typical time to live** **Live within a day** **Live within two days**


Monday 22 hours 59% 72%


Tuesday 25 hours 48% 66%


Wednesday 22 hours 55% 68%


Thursday 22 hours 51% 58%


Friday 88 hours 27% 30%


*Source: Bitrise Release Management, iOS updates submitted January to September 2026. Too few teams submit on weekends to report.*


### Friday releases mostly wait until Monday


Only one in eight Friday submissions went live over the weekend. Most of the rest went live on Monday or Tuesday, usually during working hours. That suggests teams choose not to release on weekends, as well as Apple taking its time. Either way, a fix submitted on Friday usually reaches users the following week.


### Submit between 06:00 and 18:00 UTC


Updates submitted in that window typically went live in about 22 hours. Those submitted overnight took two days or more.


### Expect July to be slow


July was the slowest month of 2026. The typical update took almost three days, and fewer than half were live within two. January and April were also slow, at about 43 hours, while other months sat at 22 to 26 hours.


## Google Play review times in 2026


Google Play review times have barely moved this year. Runway's Play Store tracker showed an average of[about 47 minutes](https://www.runway.team/playstorereviewtimes) in late October, though Google still tells developers some reviews can take[up to seven days](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9859751?hl=en) , or longer in exceptional cases. Studios waiting more than a week on Apple[told Mobilegamer.biz](https://mobilegamer.biz/app-store-review-times-are-being-dragged-down-by-a-flood-of-ai-made-apps-and-games/) their Play review times had stayed about the same.


New developers wait longest on Google Play. Personal accounts created after November 2023 have to run[a closed test with at least 12 testers](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465) for 14 days before they can apply for production access, and that application can take up to another week to review. There's no expedited review option.


We don't publish Bitrise figures for Google Play, because our Android data shows when a release is sent to Google, not when it goes live.


## What to do if your app is stuck in review


A build sitting in "Waiting for Review" for a day or two is normal, especially late in the week or in July. Apple doesn't say when to chase a slow review, so work through these in order:


1. [Check its status](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/) in the Apps section of App Store Connect. Apple emails you when it changes.
2. If it's well past the two-day mark,[contact App Review](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-review/after-submitting-for-review/contact-app-review) .
3. If a critical fix or an event date is at stake, request an expedited review (more on that below).
4. Don't cancel and resubmit to jump the queue. A new submission[starts review over](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-submissions-to-app-review/remove-a-submission-from-review) .


If the fix can't wait and your app is built with React Native, you may be able to ship it over the air instead (seeshipping fixes without waiting for review ). Our[guide to hotfixes](https://bitrise.io/guides/hotfix) explains how teams handle urgent fixes.


## How to get through App Review faster


### When to request an expedited review


Expedited review helps in an emergency, but you can't plan a release around it. You can[request one](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/) to fix a critical bug or to release in time for an event you're directly involved in. Apple grants requests as capacity allows and doesn't promise a date. One developer told WN Hub its expedited reviews still took[three to five days](https://wnhub.io/news/stores-and-publishing/item-52458) .


### Avoid the issues that slow review down


Many delays are self-inflicted. Apple says[over 40% of unresolved issues](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/) fall under guideline 2.1, App Completeness: crashes, placeholder content and missing information. A few habits help:


- **Give reviewers a way in:** if features sit behind a login, add[a working demo account](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/) in App Store Connect.
- **Answer before you resubmit:** if Apple only asks a question, reply in App Store Connect. If it flags issues, fix them first, because every resubmission[starts a new review](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-submissions-to-app-review/remove-a-submission-from-review) .
- **Use the bug-fix option:** if Apple finds new problems in a bug-fix update, it may[offer to approve the fix now](https://developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/) and let you resolve the rest in your next submission, as long as there are no legal or safety concerns. Reply to the offer in App Store Connect to accept it.


## How to plan a release around App Review


Plan for about a day, and leave three days of buffer. A third of iOS updates in our data took longer than three days, so a launch date that assumes the fastest case will slip.


- **Submit early in the week:** Monday to Thursday submissions went live in about a day.
- **Separate approval from release:** submit a few days ahead, then release on your chosen date with manual release in App Store Connect or managed publishing on Google Play.
- **Roll out in stages:** Google Play's staged rollouts limit how many users get a new build. Apple's phased release only slows automatic updates (anyone can still update manually), but it gives you time to watch crash rates and pause.
- **Track every submission in one place:** with several apps across two stores, a stuck release is easy to miss until someone asks why it isn't live.
- **Allow extra time for a first release:** Apple says some new apps need extra checks, and new Google Play personal accounts have to finish a 14-day closed test before they can publish.
- **Have a faster route for fixes:** for React Native apps, JavaScript fixes can go out over the air without review, so a bug found on Friday doesn't have to wait until next week.


[Bitrise Release Management](https://bitrise.io/platform/release-management) connects your builds to App Store Connect and Google Play and tracks each release from submission to live. You can also schedule releases and phased or staged rollouts from the same place.


## Shipping fixes without waiting for review


For React Native apps, many JavaScript bug fixes can reach users through an over-the-air (OTA) update, with no new store review. That helps most when a bad release is live and the store route would take days, like a fix submitted on a Friday.


#### Learn the basics of OTA updates


Our guides explain[what OTA updates are](https://bitrise.io/guides/ota-updates) , including[what Apple and Google allow](https://bitrise.io/blog/post/what-app-stores-allow-with-ota-updates-apple-and-google-policy-explained) , and[what CodePush is](https://bitrise.io/guides/codepush) and how it gets fixes to React Native apps.


Both stores limit what an OTA update can change.[Apple allows OTA updates](https://bitrise.io/guides/ota-updates) for fixes, improvements and content, but not for new features or a change to what the app does. Its[guideline 2.5.2](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#software-requirements) bars apps from downloading code that adds or changes features, and Apple has enforced it: in early 2026 it[blocked updates to Replit and Vibecode](https://mjtsai.com/blog/2026/03/20/updates-to-vibe-coding-apps-rejected-from-the-app-store/) and briefly removed Anything from the store. Google Play's[Device and Network Abuse policy](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9888379) bans downloading executable code from outside Google Play, but allows JavaScript that runs in a JavaScript engine or webview, which is how CodePush updates work.


**Can ship over the air** **Needs a store release**


JavaScript bug fixes Native code or native dependencies


Text, layout and image changes New permissions, such as camera or location


Small improvements to existing features React Native or native SDK upgrades


Rolling back a bad JavaScript update New features or a change of purpose

## About the data


Our iOS figures come from anonymized, aggregated Bitrise Release Management data for updates submitted to the App Store between January and September 2026.


- **What we measured:** the time from first submitting a release for App Store review to it being live on the App Store. That includes Apple's queue and review, plus any time the team waited before releasing an approved build.
- **What we left out:** demo releases, phased releases and anything that took longer than 30 days.
- **Every release had time to finish:** we only counted releases that had at least 30 days to go live, so slow recent releases aren't missing.
- **No single team skews the results:** some teams submit many apps at once, so we count each team's submissions on a given day as one data point.
- **Scope:** updates to existing iOS apps only. No brand-new apps, Mac apps or Google Play review data.
